title: Breaking bad news
stem: Relatives' room. Mr Wong, 58, came in with weight loss and jaundice. His CT shows a mass in the head of the pancreas with liver metastases; the surgeons say it is not operable. He has asked to know his results. His wife is with him. Break the news.
notes:
Checked against the SPIKES protocol (Baile et al., The Oncologist 2000), GMC guidance on decision making and consent (2020), and the Hong Kong Medical Council Code of Professional Conduct.

SPIKES: Setting (private room, sit down, no interruptions, the patient's chosen companion, tissues), Perception (what do you understand so far?), Invitation (how much detail would you like?), Knowledge (a warning shot, then plain words, small chunks, no jargon, check understanding), Emotions (acknowledge, allow silence, empathic statements), Strategy and Summary (next steps, oncology and palliative care referral, symptom control, who to contact, a follow-up plan). Honesty without destroying hope; do not give precise survival figures unless asked, and then give ranges.

In Hong Kong families sometimes ask doctors to withhold a diagnosis; the competent patient has the right to know, and here he has asked. Your notes list 'Break bad news – CA' without a script; nothing conflicts.

steps.label: Set up
steps.hint: Private room, bleep handed over, the nurse with you, tissues, enough time.

opts.t: Hand my phone to a colleague — no interruptions
Nurse Ng joins us for support
opts.mark: Brings a nurse for continuing support

opts.t: Tell him in the corridor on the way to the ward
opts.r: No privacy, no time, no chance to react.

steps.label: Talk to Mr Wong
steps.hint: Perception, invitation, warning shot, plain words, pause, empathy.

turns.line: Doctor, have the scan results come back?

opts.t: They have. Before I explain, can you tell me what you understand so far about why we did the scan?
opts.r: They said my yellow skin might be from the gallbladder… a blockage?

opts.t: Yes, you have pancreatic cancer with liver metastases.

turns.line: They said my yellow skin might be from the gallbladder… a blockage?

opts.t: How much detail would you like me to go into? Some people want everything, some just the main points.
opts.r: Tell me everything. My wife too.
opts.mark: Asks how much information he wants

turns.line: Tell me everything. My wife too.

opts.t: I'm afraid the results are not what we hoped. [pause] The scan shows a growth in the pancreas, which is blocking the bile duct. It looks like a cancer, and it has spread to the liver.
opts.mark: Gives a warning shot, then the news in plain language

opts.t: There is a hypodense lesion in the pancreatic head with hepatic metastatic deposits.
opts.r: I don't understand any of that.

opts.t: [Pause] This must be a terrible shock. [Silence] The surgeons have looked carefully; because it has spread, an operation would not cure it. But there is a lot we can do.
opts.mark: Acknowledges emotion, allows silence, answers honestly

opts.r: How can you be so cold?

opts.t: That's hard to say for any one person. It's likely to be months rather than years, but the oncology team can tell you more once they know how you respond to treatment.
opts.r: …Months. OK. Thank you for being honest.
opts.mark: Answers prognosis honestly with a range, not a number

opts.t: Don't think about that — stay positive!
A stent can relieve the jaundice and itch; the oncologists will discuss chemotherapy; the palliative care team will help with symptoms. I'll see you on the ward tomorrow. What questions do you have?
opts.r: My wife and I need to think. Thank you, doctor.
opts.mark: Gives a plan, referral and follow-up, and invites questions

steps.label: Mrs Wong asks to speak to you outside
steps.hint: Respect the patient's confidentiality and his wishes; support her too.

turns.line: Doctor, please don't tell him any more bad news. Tell me first in future.

opts.t: I understand you want to protect him. He has asked to be told himself, so I'll keep being honest with him — gently. With his permission, we can include you in every conversation.
opts.r: …All right. As long as you're kind to him.
opts.mark: Respects the patient's autonomy while supporting the family

opts.t: Of course, I'll tell you and keep him in the dark.

qs.q: What does the P in SPIKES stand for?
qs.a: Perception — what the patient already understands
A brief phrase that signals bad news is coming

qs.q: A family asks you to withhold a diagnosis from a competent adult who wants to know. You…
qs.a: Explain that the patient has a right to the information he asks for
wrong: Refer to the ethics committee before speaking

qs.a: Pause, acknowledge the emotion, offer tissues
wrong: Move on quickly to the plan

qs.q: How to answer 'How long do I have?'
qs.a: Honestly, with a range and uncertainty

badge.name: SPIKES
badge.flavor: Ask, warn, tell plainly, pause, plan.

options: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy/Summary
Situation, Plan, Information, Knowledge, Empathy, Safety
Silence, Pause, Inform, Kindness, Explain, Stop
Setting, Prognosis, Investigation, Knowledge, Emotion, Support

cards.q: The first question when breaking news is usually…
options: What do you understand so far?
Who is your next of kin?

cards.q: Medical jargon when breaking bad news should be…
A competent adult wants to know his diagnosis; the family objects. The doctor should…
options: Respect the patient's wish to know
cards.why: Autonomy and confidentiality belong to the patient.

cards.q: A good ending to a bad-news consultation includes…
options: A plan, a follow-up, and an invitation for questions
